A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEAPS research work. Their complete text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material relocated in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original Ising simulations comparing network architectures, effective sample size, magnetization, and correlations against Glauber dynamics (Section 11, Figure 4).

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds critical-temperature Ising and Potts results, AIS comparisons, and DISCS sampler comparisons (Figures 4–9).

M1.justification: The CTMC sampler, importance-weight updates, PINN objective, and locally equivariant architectures remain unchanged. Section 9 reorganizes the existing prediction-head/token-projector explanation; the training and sampling algorithms are relocated or renumbered without procedural changes.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates a 15-by-15 Ising model at J=0.4 and beta=0.7. v2 retains this setting and adds critical-temperature Ising evaluation at J=1 and beta=0.4407, plus Potts-model sampling. This substantially broadens the target distributions and difficulty regimes actually evaluated.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained architecture variants, no-transport control, and Glauber reference, v2 adds DISCS comparisons containing hammingball, randomwalk, gibbs, blockgibbs, gwg, path_auxiliary, dlmc, and dmala (Figures 5 and 9). These are evaluated comparators, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: New comparisons sweep AIS budgets from 10^3 to 10^6 steps against 100-step LEAPS and introduce ESS per function evaluation. Section 11 also changes the reported annealing prescription from linear J_t, mu_t, and beta_t starting at J_0=0 to linear beta_t. This documents a protocol revision without establishing that the retained ablation was rerun.

E4.justification: The original depth, attention-versus-convolution, and no-transport analyses are retained in Figure 7. v2 adds AIS step-budget sensitivity curves (Figures 4 and 6) and extends magnetization/correlation fidelity checks to critical-temperature Ising (Figure 8), without introducing new component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, or formal uncertainty-estimation procedures. The uncertainty displays in v1 Figure 4 remain in v2 Figure 7; the new benchmarks do not introduce confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds reported LEAPS ESS values of approximately 68% for critical Ising and 20% for Potts, AIS budget curves, DISCS rankings, and critical-Ising observable agreement. These are additional results under new conditions, not improvements over v1 at matched settings. One inconsistency remains: Section 11 says AIS reaches similar Ising ESS near 10^6 steps, but Figure 4 shows approximately 0.29 versus LEAPS's approximately 0.68.

T1.justification: New Appendix E.1 adds Proposition E.1 and a Stone–Weierstrass-based proof of universal approximation using polynomial features and locally invariant heads, extending the architectural expressivity analysis. Section 4 also restores the missing free-energy derivative in the derivation of Equation 10, and Appendix C removes a stray residual identity.

C1.justification: The abstract's scientific claims and the five introductory contributions remain unchanged: CTMC transport, path-space importance weights, PINN training, locally equivariant networks, and high-dimensional validation. The rewritten discussion emphasizes network design without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets one-way rates as kinetically favorable and emphasizes more expressive, scalable architectures as future work. Figures 5 and 9 explicitly qualify the comparisons: LEAPS counts neural-network evaluations, MCMC counts energy calls, and their ESS measurements differ.

D1.justification: v2 adds code-access information in the abstract and Appendix G and directs readers to DISCS for Potts details. Existing architecture sizes and kernel settings move from Appendix G.1 into Figure 7's caption. Section 9 drops the explicitly stated all-ones initialization; no alternative initialization is specified.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to DISCS, autoregressive statistical-physics samplers by Wu and McNaughton, and discrete-diffusion optimization work by Sanokowski. These expand the relevant comparisons and context while retaining the original positioning relative to transport methods and CTMC generative models.

P1.justification: Sections 9, 11, and 12 receive localized restructuring and rewriting. Ising definitions move to Appendix G, architecture details move into a caption, and training pseudocode moves after the references. Most theoretical exposition and the overall section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation expands substantially with AIS curves, ESS/ESS-per-evaluation bar charts, and critical-Ising observable plots (Figures 4–6, 8–9). The original Figure 4 becomes Figure 7 with an expanded caption, and training pseudocode is relocated. Conceptual Figures 1–3 are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 improves support beyond v1's single Ising setting through critical-regime validation, Potts experiments, an expressivity proof, and code-access information. However, the comparative-efficiency evidence remains limited: DISCS comparisons use different ESS definitions and function-call costs, and the Ising AIS prose contradicts Figure 4. These limitations temper the empirical expansion, leaving a clear but limited net improvement in overall quality.
